Items.Authors: Eder Martioli, Bruno V. Castilho, Jesulino B. Santos, Orlando Verducci, Flavio F. Ribeiro, Clemens D. Gneiding, Marcio V. Arruda, Francisco Rodrigues, Luciano Fraga, Leandro H. Santos, Josimar A. Rosa, Denis V. Bernardes, Vanessa B. Macanham, Antonio Cesar Oliveira, Bernard Delabre, Décio Ferreira, Felipe Navarete, Julio F. Silva, Murilo Marinello, Vinicius L. Pimentel, Isabel Aleman, Danilo A. Gonçalves
Items.Title: ECHARPE: the high resolution échelle spectrograph for the Pico dos Dias Observatory P&E Telescope
Items.Abstract: ECHARPE is a new fiber-fed, high-resolution échelle spectrograph for the 1.6-m Perkin & Elmer telescope at the Observatório do Pico dos Dias (OPD/LNA), Brazil. Designed as a bench-mounted and environmentally controlled instrument, it delivers broad visible-band coverage (380-900nm) with a resolving power of R~50,000, enabling precise radial velocity and stellar abundance analyses. This contribution summarizes the main characteristics and design choices of the instrument, including its optical layout, mechanical architecture, fiber-injection system, and calibration unit. We describe the final construction phase now underway, focusing on the integration of the optical bench, alignment of opto-mechanical assemblies, and implementation of the control and data-acquisition systems. We present initial laboratory results, including preliminary spectral measurements, stability tests, and throughput estimates. Installation is planned for 2026, enhancing the spectroscopic capabilities at OPD.

Items.Authors: Shubham Ghatul, Rekhesh Mohan, Jayant Murthy, Margarita Safonova, Praveen Kumar, Shubhangi Jain, Mahesh S. Babu
Items.Title: Near Ultraviolet Transient Explorer (NUTEx): instrument design, calibration, and testing of a CubeSat-based NUV imaging payload for transient sky surveys
Items.Abstract: We present the Near Ultraviolet Transient Explorer (NUTEx), a CubeSat-based compact imaging payload designed for wide-field NUV sky surveys in the 200–300 nm band. The instrument uses a 146 mm Ritchey–Chrétien optical system with a solar-blind MCP detector and in-house-developed readout electronics, providing a 4° field of view, 13″ resolution, and a peak effective area of 15 cm² at 260 nm. NUTEx is optimized to monitor fast NUV transients, including flaring stars, M-dwarfs, and supernovae, particularly in bright sky regions avoided by earlier missions. The payload emphasizes modular, low-cost subsystem development using COTS components that satisfy spaceflight requirements. We are currently assembling the flight model and testing the engineering model for qualification. In this paper we present the instrument calibration and performance results following these tests, demonstrating NUTEx’s readiness for its planned Q4-2026 launch.

Items.Authors: Kieran Mulholland, Jens Knudstrup, Gerard Zins
Items.Title: New developments in the use of the Aravis library for GigE technical detectors in VLTSW
Items.Abstract: The Technical Detector Control Software (TDCS) is used by the European Southern Observatory’s (ESO) Very Large Telescope (VLT) to control GenICam-compliant detectors using the GigE Vision interface, usually making use of the Aravis open-source library. Two new features of TDCS are currently in development. The first is the introduction of support for the Pleora iPORT CL-GigE External Frame Grabber. The second is the introduction of a contextless encapsulation of Aravis in modern C++20, allowing both the VLT and ELT software stacks to use the same implementation of the Aravis library for GigE Vision devices. This will significantly reduce the maintenance and development requirements of both VLT and ELT as both telescopes make use of different detectors and use cases.

Items.Authors: Kun Chen, Wen Chen, Yingquan Yang, Xuliang Duan, Yang Gao, Genjian Qin, Xinyu Liu, Duojin Zheng, Siran Ding, Xu Wu, Dongxiao Xu, Qixing Wang, Jiangjiang Huang, Yifei Wang, Na Meng, Zhiming Cai, Rong Shu, Jian Ge, Hui Zhang, Yongshuai Zhang, Weicheng Zang, Hongjing Yang, Shude Mao, Yutian Fu, Yonghe Chen, Feng Dong, Zongxi Song, Wei Gao, Hongfei Zhang, Jian Wang, Lianguo Wang, Yongmei Wang
Items.Title: Progress of the Earth 2.0 space spacecraft system design
Items.Abstract: The Earth 2.0 (ET) mission is a next-generation Chinese space mission to detect thousands of Earth-sized planets, including habitable Earth-like planets orbiting solar type stars (Earth 2.0s), cold low-mass planets, and free floating planets. The ET mission will enter its Phase C study in 2026. During the Phase B study, detailed design and optimization of the spacecraft system were carried out, and several key aspects were updated to better fulfill the scientific requirements. In particular, the pointing stability requirement has been increased by more than one order of magnitude. This paper presents the progress in the ET spacecraft system design, covering the overall configuration, pointing stability control, scientific data download, and other aspects.

Items.Authors: Laurane Fréour, Bodo Ziegler, Roland Bacon, Sofia Randlich, Etienne Burtin, Arlette Pecontal, Philippe Dierickx, David Lee, Vincenzo Mainieri, Paolo Franzetti, Alessandro Meoli, Peter Weilbacher, Dimitri Buffat, Simone D'Auria, Letizia P. Cassarà, Corentin Cudennec
Items.Title: Sustainability as a design parameter in the early development of the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope
Items.Abstract: The proposed Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a next-generation telescope facility with a 12-meter primary mirror that may be operational in the 2040s, is integrating sustainable considerations from the early design stage.    Our preliminary analysis identifies two primary sources of environmental impact that can be mitigated during the design process.    First, we are conducting a life-cycle assessment to quantify the environmental impact of the ~600 detectors and their cooling systems across their lifecycles for three options.     Second, the WST is expected to produce ~1-3 PB/year, requiring careful evaluation of data processing and storage strategies. We explore approaches to monitor and reduce the carbon footprint and overall environmental impact related to data management.

Items.Authors: Elena Tonucci, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Kyle van Gorkom, Olivier Guyon, Alexander D. Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Joseph D. Long, Jennifer R. Lumbres, Matthijs Mars, Eden A. McEwen, Avalon L. McLeod, María Eugenia Redondo González, Lauren H. Schatz, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: First on-sky focal plane wavefront control demonstration with the self-coherent camera
Items.Abstract: High-contrast imaging instruments are limited by wavefront errors originating from non-common path aberrations creating quasi-static speckles that mimic companions. The Self-Coherent Camera (SCC) exploits the light incoherence between star and companion to sense the speckle field. Starlight hits a coronagraph mask and is diffracted outside the Lyot stop, where it is filtered by a pinhole to create a reference beam. This, recombined with the leaked starlight, creates interference fringes affecting starlight only. The mask was designed and manufactured in-house at Leiden University with Nanoscribe, a micro-3D-printer that uses two-photon polymerization. We present the first on-sky closed-loop wavefront control demonstration of the Fast Atmospheric SCC Technique (FAST) with MagAO-X, the extreme adaptive optics instrument for the 6.5m Magellan Clay telescope at Las Campanas Observatory. We show contrast performance with and without active wavefront control and post-processed results.

Items.Authors: Longxiang Li, Qiang Cheng, Runmu Cheng, Xingchang Li, Lingtong Zhang, Donglin Xue, Xuejun Zhang
Items.Title: Surface quality and shape accuracy control in manufacturing large-aperture optical mirrors
Items.Abstract: High precision manufacturing of large aperture complex curved surface optical elements is one of the core technologies in the development of modern large-scale optical systems. This report introduces the achievements of the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CIOMP) in the manufacturing of large-aperture aspheric mirrors, including the world's largest monolithic silicon carbide mirror and the development of high-precision manufacturing and testing equipment. This report also presents the latest advancements in optical fabrication based on industrial robots, analyze the key challenges and core solutions, and validate high-precision optical manufacturing can be achieved using low-precision industrial robots. Furthermore, the strategies for the rapid generation of high-quality optical surfaces, controlling the defect, are analyzed. Finally, this report reviews the international collaboration between the CIOMP and Europe.

Items.Authors: Thibault Pichon, Clara Bataillon, Jérôme Amiaux, Pierre-Olivier Lagage, Marc Ollivier, Benoît Horeau, Christophe Cara, Grégory Kaszubiak, François Visticot, Léna Provost
Items.Title: Gain stability of the ARIEL-AIRS H1RG infrared detectors
Items.Abstract: AIRS is the infrared spectroscopic instrument of the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large-survey (ARIEL). The mission is dedicated to the study of the exoplanet’s atmosphere. AIRS will perform spectroscopic measurements from the near-infrared domain to the long-wave infrared domain. The instrument relies on the use of two H1RG detectors.   ARIEL will rely on transit spectroscopy to probe exoplanets’ atmosphere. The AIRS acquisition, based on tailored electronics chain, has been designed from inception to be extremely stable, to reduce the sensitivity of the acquisition to thermal variations of the environement. During EM characterization phase, detector sensitivity with applied biases has been assessed. This paper will focus on the stability of the full AIRS acquisition chain. We will provide a bried description of its architecture. Then, we will describe the method used to characterize the sensitivity of the acquisition chain. Results will be presented and discussed

Items.Authors: Nicole Melso, Haeun Chung, Daniel DeFelippis, Erika Hamden, Keri Hoadley, Drew Miles, David Schiminovich
Items.Title: The MgnoLya UV SmallSat: mapping Mg II and Lyα emission around nearby galaxies
Items.Abstract: MgnoLya is a UV SmallSat mission concept designed to map cold gas (∼104 K) and dust around nearby galaxies.  MgnoLya targets low-ionization resonant line emission produced by recombination and scattering, specifically  Mg II (λλ2796, 2803) and Lyα (λ1218). Both of these lines provide key insights into the structure and kinematics  of the circumgalactic medium, and they can be targeted in tandem with an optimized optical design. Observations  of these tracers at low redshift have been hindered by the need for sensitive UV measurements of faint emission  and by contamination from the strong geocoronal Lyα line. The MgnoLya instrument design is optimized for  low surface brightness observations while maintaining a moderate spectral resolution to distinguish kinematic  and line diagnostic signatures. We present the mission overview, highlighting key technologies including high-  efficiency, low-scatter gratings and low-noise skipper CCD detectors that allow us to push towards fainter limits.

Items.Authors: Paolo G. Calisse
Items.Title: The two-way relationship between astronomical facilities and the climate crisis
Items.Abstract: The construction and operation of astronomical observatories can have a significant impact on their surrounding environment. Conversely, climate change also affects observatory operations, influencing both risk levels and data quality. This study investigates this two-way relationship and proposes the creation of a global forum where different facilities can share experiences and discuss strategies to enhance the sustainability of their projects.

Items.Authors: Gabriel Rodrigues Santos, Eduardo Zancul
Items.Title: Assessing the cost-effectiveness of telescope arrays with commercial components: a framework based on signal-to-noise ratio and cost tradeoff
Items.Abstract: Telescope arrays are increasingly relevant for low-surface-brightness (LSB) photometry and transient detection and follow up. However, their cost-effectiveness has been less explored, which can lead to suboptimal investment decisions. This work models and compares commercially available components (telescopes with apertures from 5cm to 2.5m, cameras and filters) with a framework based around a signal to noise ratio calculator fed with component technical specifications and cost data. We tested three use cases: true-colour RGB imaging, photometry in Sloan g'r' bands, and transient detection in the clear band. Results show that an array of amateur telescopes (30-40cm) can outperform single-aperture systems of equivalent etendue or total cost. This can guide the selection of components for modular and scalable array design.

Items.Authors: Florent Mallet, Elise VERNET, Pablo Zuluaga Ramirez, Constanza Araujo Hauck, Marc Cayrel, Fabien Ciapponi, Claire Lamour, Elodie Milhiet, Xavier Tonnellier, Pablo Lefevre, Alexandre Potier, Alexandra Guggenheim, Marc Ferrato, Jean-Marc Boitrel
Items.Title: Manufacturing the ELT M5 Blank Mirror, a world of challenges
Items.Abstract: The M5 mirror, a 2.2 × 2.7 m² flat, fast tip-tilt mirror made of silicon carbide (SiC), is part the adaptive optics system of the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).  We will focus on the unique manufacturing challenges of the M5 blank mirror. Producing even a single petal required the largest raw SiC block ever made. But the main technical difficulty was combining chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of SiC - essential for optical performance - with brazing technology, necessary to achieve the mirror’s dimensions. This combination demanded innovative improvements and rigorous qualification processes. The development was a collaborative effort involving ESO, Safran Reosc, Mersen Gennevilliers, and Mersen Boostec, ensuring consistent polishing behavior across all petals.  Finally, we will discuss upcoming developments for the second M5 blank mirror, the spare one, which will benefit from an improved SiC CVD layer and enhanced brazing material, both specifically qualified for this application.

Items.Authors: Alan Vasquez Soto, Nicholas Law, Hank Corbett, Alex Bucheli, Glenn Walters
Items.Title: Building an 8-m class observatory on startup timelines: Argus Array project management and current status
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array is an 8-meter-class telescope array monitoring 8,000 square degrees simultaneously using 1,200 individual 28-cm telescopes. With first-light targeted for mid-2027, the project demonstrates an approach for delivering observatory facilities through rapid prototyping, integrated technical leadership, and flexible project management. Our approach combines phase-gate milestones with flexibility to redesign systems at critical phases, enabled by in-house prototyping on week-scale iterations, flat management structure, and iterative requirements discovery. Senior technical leadership embedded across subsystems enables rapid identification of design elements impacting science performance, which enabled a design pivot when initial mount architectures proved cost-prohibitive. By mid-2026, we expect to have broken ground and completed integrated system demonstration. We present our project management methodology, systems engineering approach, current status, and lessons learned.

Items.Authors: Sylvain Oberti, Johann Kolb, Jean-Baptiste Lebouquin, Anthony Berdeu, Julien Woillez, Henri Bonnet, Pavel Shchekaturov, Guillaume Bourdarot, Frank Eisenhauer, Frederic Gonté
Items.Title: GRAVITY+ adaptive optics
Items.Abstract: GRAVITY+ is an upgrade of the VLTI facility, providing unprecented spatial resolution and sensitivity. One of the project's objectives was to replace the low order NGS SCAO systems (MACAO and CIAO) with four high order AO modules incorporated in the Coude train of each VLT: GRAVITY Plus AO (GPAO). This talk will present GPAO focusing on the AO design, highlighting technical peculiarities and novel approaches of interest for future ELT AO systems. First, the NGS AO modes in visible and infrared wavelengths will be described in terms of implementation, on sky performance and scientific impact, including the high contrast applications. Then, we will introduce the recently commissioned LGS AO modes starting with the performance of the LGS systems, a copy of the ELT ones. The delivered wavefront correction will be shown as a function of NGS magnitude. Finally, we will highlight some key technical aspects relevant for furture AO systems, notably the Rayleigh background scattering management.

Items.Authors: Lisa A. Crause, Willem J. van der Westhuizen, Danièl Groenewald, Encarni Romero Colmenero, Daniel L. Holdsworth, Paul Groot, Tasheen Naicker, Malcolm C. Scarrott, Sam Ndumo, Kathryn Rosie, Moses K. Mogotsi, Alexei Kniazev, Etienne L. Simon, Eben P. Wiid, Nico van der Merwe, Sabyasachi Chattopadhyay, Antoine Mahoro, Rudi Kuhn
Items.Title: Southern African Large Telescope (SALT) instrumentation update
Items.Abstract: We report on the various instrument upgrades and development projects underway at the Southern African Large Telescope (SALT). The prime focus tracker assembly carries the four-mirror spherical aberration corrector (SAC), the coatings of which are failing. This severely limits telescope performance, so we are embarking on a project to replace the corrector. The current optical prescription will be retained, but the new opto-mechanical structure will make provision for routine maintenance. Assorted upgrades to the instruments are also planned or in progress. These include: the addition of a custom-built laser frequency comb and precision radial velocity pipeline for the fibre-fed high-resolution spectrograph; a new detector and novel slit-mask integral field units (IFU) for the prime focus spectrograph; a new acquisition camera for the telescope and hardware to monitor telescope and instrument throughput. Lastly, we will need to replace our infrared spectrograph's damaged H2RG detector.

Items.Authors: Davide Sisana, Marta Maria Civitani, Laura Proserpio, Stefano Basso, Vincenzo Cotroneo, Kotish Grover, Briana L. Indahl, Brian T. Fleming, Timothy Hellickson
Items.Title: The Hettrick-Bowyer EUV grazing incidence telescope for the MANTIS CubeSat: from design to engineering model
Items.Abstract: MANTIS (Monitoring Activity of Nearby sTars with uv Imaging and Spectroscopy) mission is a 16U CubeSat led by the LASP. The EUV telescope of MANTIS – contributed and realized by INAF/OABrera - is based on the Hettrick-Bowyer optical design: a parabolic primary mirror (105 mm inner diameter) and an elliptical secondary mirror (16 mm inner diameter) are confocal in a 100 µm pinhole.   The telescope's opto-mechanical design is hereby presented, along with the Finite Element Analysis performed to validate its structural, thermal, and dynamic behavior. Moreover, the tolerance analysis and the expected optical performance are described, providing the necessary requirements for manufacturing and alignment of the optical components. Lastly, we show the results achieved with the aluminum engineering model, which was manufactured and used for a comprehensive Assembly, Integration, and Test campaign, by means of a UV optical bench, to assess the alignment procedure.

Items.Authors: Bart Speet
Items.Title: VLT 8 ELT laser projection system status update

Items.Authors: Sebastian Aranda
Items.Title: What is LOVE: learnings and challenges in developing a real time monitoring system for observatory operations
Items.Abstract: The LSST Operations and Visualization Environment (LOVE) is the main monitoring software system at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, created to observe its state and environmental conditions in real-time. Connected to all subsystems—from the telescope itself to facility microphones—LOVE displays telemetry in an intuitive format for real-time operations. This paper describes the nine-year development process of this system, involving diverse teams of developers, Observing Specialists, engineers, and scientists. We share key lessons and challenges faced across its life cycle, from initial design to long-term maintenance. Specifically, we address how we scaled the architecture to support massive sensor connections, broadcasting data to multiple clients simultaneously. We discuss crucial aspects of building real-time interfaces, maintaining requirement flexibility, and collaborating with users to ensure useful workflows. The paper covers UI/UX, system performance, and evolution management.

Items.Authors: Lee D. Feinberg
Items.Title: Startup telescope: deconstructing flagships missions to go faster and bolder
Items.Abstract: Over the past few years, much work has gone into applying lessons from previous flagship missions to future missions. These lessons learned include more emphasis on the early maturation of mission concepts in a holistic way to assure the plan developed is fully executable and using servicing to reduce programmatic risk. However, those lessons learned were based on an assumed set of constraints in the areas of program management, system engineering, mission assurance, procurement and human relations. In this talk we deconstruct these constraints and assess whether approaches used by technology startups can be applied. In this talk we will review how technology startups and commercial companies achieve speed and flexibility by focusing on value added activities with minimal wait-states or bureaucracy. With those lessons in mind, we will assess whether the assumed constraints are value-added to building hardware that is faster (and thus cheaper) to enable bolder science.

Items.Authors: Paul Eccleston, Andrew Caldwell, Georgia Bishop, Lucile Desjonquères, Rachel Drummond, Alex Davidson, Martin Whalley, Martin Caldwell, Chris Pearson, Caroline Simpson, Lee Hamer, Sandy Fok, Davide Bruzzi, Mark Anderson, Katherine Ostojic, Pranav Umesh, Salma Fahmy, Gareth Rees, Giovanna Tinetti, Enzo Pascale, Giorgio Savini, Gianluca Morgante, Mauro Focardi, Marc Ollivier, Miroslaw Rataj, Giuseppi Malaguti, Andrea Tozzi, Paolo Chioetto, Paolo Picchi, Emanuele Pace, Paola Zuppella, Giampaolo Preti, Jose Gomez, Christophe Serre, Javier Perez Alvarez, Andres Garcia Pérez, Alejandro Fernandez, Neil Bowles, Jerome Martignac, Michel Berthé, Benoît Horeau, Martin Crook, Matthew Hills, Charles Padley, Semu Mäkinen, János Szőke, Zsolt Kovacs, Mateusz Sobiecki, Konrad Skup, Roland Ottensamer, Gerald Mösenlechner, Warren Holmes, Renaud Goullioud, Guillermo Guinea, Søren Møller Pedersen, Lukáš Steiger, Umberto Barozzi, Andrea Paternoster, Lorenzo Maddii, Alessandro Bini, Ludovic Puig, Delphine Jollet, Anders Svedevall, Thierry Tirolien, Jean-Christophe Salvignol, Jean-Philippe Halain
Items.Title: The Ariel payload: design progress and structural model outcomes
Items.Abstract: The Ariel space mission will characterize spectroscopically the atmospheres of a large and diverse sample of hundreds of exoplanets. Ariel is an ESA Medium class science mission (M4) with a Payload provided by a consortium of national funding agencies in ESA member states, plus contributions from NASA, the CSA and JAXA. The payload is based on a 1-meter class telescope operated at below 60K, built all in Aluminium, which feeds two science instruments; a multi-channel guider, photometer and low-resolution spectrometer instrument (the FGS) and a medium resolution spectroscopy instrument (AIRS).  This paper provides an overview of the design of the overall payload for the Ariel mission, with a focus on the design updates of the Payload since the payload PDR in 2023, along with the outcomes and lessons learnt from the build of the payload module Structural Model (pSM) in 2025 and the mechanical environmental testing of this pSM in Q1 2026.

Items.Authors: Jared R. Males, Joseph D. Long, Sebastiaan Haffert, Olivier Guyon, Vincent Déo, Kyle Van Gorkom, Irina Stefan, Parker Johnson, Rico Landman, Ewan Douglas, Laird M. Close
Items.Title: The eXtreme Wavefront Control Toolkit: High-Contrast Imaging Instrument Control for Ground and Space-Based Coronagraphs
Items.Abstract: The eXtreme Wavefront Control Toolkit (XWCTk) is the instrument control software developed for the MagAO-X ExAO instrument. The XWCTk provides configuration, logging, distributed inter-process communication (IPC) with INDI and low-latency IPC with ImageStreamIO. On the MagAO-X instrument, every detector is a potential wavefront sensor to control three separate deformable mirrors. MagAO-X runs at up to 3.6 Khz on the 2000 actuator main AO system, and over 8 kHz on the low-order coronagraph system. A core design principle of the XWCTk is that all data can be saved all the time using a custom lossless compression. Remote operation (e.g. Tucson, Arizona to LCO, Chile) is routine. The XWCTk is under continuous development for MagAO-X, and will be adapted for GMagAO-X, the planned first-light ExAO coronagraph for the GMT. Additionally, XWCTk is the baseline for a space high contrast imaging instrument, and as such ongoing development is focused on automation for robust operation in flight.

Items.Authors: Fadi Atallah, Hongyu Li, Anthony Beaucamp, David Walker, Richard Freeman
Items.Title: Slurry processing for longer-lasting high-power laser optics
Items.Abstract: In megajoule laser optics, it’s rarely the surface figure that ends an optic’s life - it’s the hidden SSD beneath it. These tiny crack pockets trap photo-absorbing impurities, which grow under repeated shots. We present a nanosilica-diamond slurry that reduces SSD to 150 nm and surface roughness to 4 Å.

Items.Authors: T. W. Buggey, K. D. Stefanov, J. Requena, J. Ivory, T. Arnold, A. D. Holland, D. Jordan, M. R. Soman, D. J. Hall
Items.Title: CIS321: a large-format, monolithic CMOS image sensor for soft x-ray astronomy
Items.Abstract: During early development of ESA’s M7 candidate mission, THESEUS, it was identified that the focal plane of the SXI could only be cooled to -40 °C. This single requirement meant that the go-to detector, CCDs, could not be used, and alternative technology developments were required. The Centre for Electronic imaging, in collaboration with Teledyne e2v, and funded by ESA, designed, manufactured, and characterized the CIS221-X, the world’s first X-ray optimised CIS. This talk will describe the preliminary results of the next phase of detector development, the 4.5 × 9cm CIS321.

Items.Authors: Volker Heinz, Bernhard Lopez, David Bristow, Vanessa Montes, Uwe Steinborn, Patricia Marquez, Gareth Hughes, Markus Gaug
Items.Title: The CTAO construction programme: building a multi-site Gamma-ray Observatory
Items.Abstract: The scope of the CTAO construction programme encompasses a wide range of activities of the CTAO central organization to prepare both observatory sites in La Palma and at the Paranal Observatory in Chile for the operation of the telescope arrays.  One of the key elements is the planning and construction of the site infrastructure for CTAO-South, including civil works, electrical distribution, IT network and on-site data centres, and other facilities for the construction and operations phase. Other than in the South at CTAO-N the site infrastructure is being provided by the Instituto de Astrofisica de Canarias (IAC), according to the requirements and specifications of the observatory.  The programme supports the deployment, AIV and commissioning of telescopes and calibration equipment, performs the system integration and prepares the sites for intermediate array configurations and supports operations.  Current planning foresees the completion of the construction phase in 2029.

Items.Authors: Celeste Elizalde Flores, Brian Fleming, Alex Haughton, Kevin France, Randy McEntaffer, Fabien Grisé, Dimitry Vorobiev
Items.Title: The MOBIUS sounding rocket: integral-field and dual-octave spectroscopy to probe galactic feedback mechanisms in the near- and far-UV
Items.Abstract: Integral-field unit (IFU) spectroscopy—first demonstrated on the INFUSE sounding rocket using an image slicer and 26 high-efficiency UV gratings—will be extended to enable more detailed measurements of the spectral morphology of galaxies. The Multi-Octave Bandpass Integral-field Ultraviolet Spectrograph (MOBIUS) represents the next generation of UV IFU instrumentation, providing simultaneous FUV and NUV capabilities. The MOBIUS design incorporates large 50 × 50 mm sealed-tube cross-strip (XS) detectors with newly developed ASIC readout electronics that offer lower power consumption and improved suitability for spaceflight compared to the system used for INFUSE. In addition, MOBIUS will employ etched-silicon gratings fabricated at Pennsylvania State University, which provide enhanced aberration control in the NUV channels and are expected to deliver lower scatter and higher efficiency than conventional blazed gratings.

Items.Authors: Avinash Surendran, Maxwell Service, Jacques R. Delorme, Marcos van Dam, Carlos M. Correia, Eduardo Marin, Antonin Bouchez, Peter Wizinowich, Sylvain Cetre, Uriel Conod, Jacob Taylor, Scott Lilley, Ed Wetherell, Jessica Lu, Noah Stiegler, Anna Pusack, Zoe Haggard, Will Gauvin, Julien T. Bernard, Dietrich Pescoller, Roberto Biasi
Items.Title: On-sky capabilities and performance of the Keck All sky Precision Adaptive optics system
Items.Abstract: The Keck All sky Precision Adaptive optics (KAPA) project upgrades the Keck I adaptive optics system to enable laser tomography using a four laser guide star (LGS) asterism. KAPA is now in operation in both laser tomography adaptive and ground-layer adaptive optics modes to optimize correction on-axis or over the science field of view of the camera. The use of four LGSs, in conjunction with a tomographic reconstructor and pseudo open-loop control, leads to a significant reduction in wavefront error. We describe the upgrades to the laser, diffractive optical elements, real-time controller, high-level software, wavefront sensor optics and camera, and calibration unit. We describe the development of the tomographic algorithm and real-time implementation. By comparing the on-sky image quality with that obtained using a single LGS we clearly demonstrate the benefits of laser tomography, a technology which is crucial to the success of the next generation of extremely large telescopes.

Items.Authors: Juan Cózar-Castellano, Marta Belío-Asín, Ángel Mato-Martínez, Alejandro Mahy Soler Trujillo, Miguel Núñez Cagigal, Nauzet Vega, Cristina Padilla-Hernández, Mary Barreto, Héctor Lacasta, Juan Miguel Gonzalez, Marta García-Cosío, Iago Funes Vecino, Adrián García-Hidalgo Baeza, Manuel Collados
Items.Title: Heat Rejecter mirror in additive manufacturing for the European Solar Telescope
Items.Abstract: The European Solar Telescope (EST) is a 4.2-m solar telescope, currently in the preliminary design phase. The Heat Rejecter is a mirror with a central hole that lies at the prime focus of the telescope (F1) and operates as a first field stop of the optical system. The Heat Rejecter aims to reject the solar radiation outside the selected field of view to avoid extra thermal load in the following optical elements and the seeing degradation, avoiding the development of thermal plumes in the optical path. This paper shows the status of the Heat Rejecter preliminary design.

Items.Authors: Takashi Hattori, Naoyuki Tamura, Yosuke Minowa, Shintaro Koshida, Hirofumi Okita, Olivier Guyon, Matthew Wung
Items.Title: Instrumentation at the Subaru Telescope
Items.Abstract: We present the current status and future plan of the instruments at the Subaru Telescope.  Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS), the fiber-fed multi-object spectrograph with 1.3 degrees FoV, was recently given the Hawaiian name “ʻŌnohiʻula”. It equipped all hard-ware components in August 2024, and started the science operation in March 2025.  For the next generation wide-field facility instrument ULTIMATE-Subaru, the Ground Layer Adaptive Optics (GLAO) system and the Wide-Field Imager (WFI) are now in the phases of the final and detailed design, respectively.  For the existing facility AO system AO188/3k, the upgrade of the deformable mirror (DM) to ALPAO 64x64 DM was done in 2024, and the implementations of new wavefront sensors have been ongoing. In addition, the installation of the Nasmyth Beam Switcher (NBS) was done in 2025, which made the operation of the downstream instruments of AO188/3k more flexible and effective.

Items.Authors: Dallas Wulf, Matt Dobbs, Brian Hoff, Michael Rupen, Kendrick Smith, Keith Vanderlinde
Items.Title: Project management of the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector
Items.Abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector (CHORD) is a new drift-scan radio interferometer operating from 300–1500 MHz, optimized for 21cm intensity mapping, 21cm galaxy detection, pulsars, and transient detection and localization. The full instrument will feature a core array of 512 six-meter dishes, plus two 64-dish outriggers at several thousand kilometer baselines. The project is nearing completion of the first 64-dish sub-array, which will enable commissioning activities to begin in parallel with the remaining construction. In this presentation, we discuss the project management framework that has enabled us to navigate the logistical challenges of a fixed-budget, fixed-timeline research infrastructure project through a period of significant global economic and technological volatility.

Items.Authors: Petr Kubánek
Items.Title: Rubin Observatory’s telescope & site software: developing, commissioning, and operating software for a new survey telescope
Items.Abstract: Vera C. Rubin Observatory is an operational integrated observatory located at Cerro Pachon in Chile. It is composed of two telescopes: The Simony Survey 8.4m telescope and a smaller 1.2m Auxiliary telescope. The observatory is complemented with various monitoring systems and sensors, enabling it to reach its full potential, both with an exquisite image quality and high efficiency. The goal of the observatory is to collect scans of the visible sky every ~3 nights for 10 years, mapping the universe. This shall enable discoveries of both expected, but not confirmed, events, as well as new, unknown phenomena. The paper describes the design and implementation of the control and image processing software that orchestrates the instrument operation and enables automated data acquisition and analysis. The presented software framework ensures robust system control, real-time image handling, and flexible integration with future hardware and algorithmic upgrades.

Items.Authors: Paolo Picchi, Andrea Tozzi, Anna Brucalassi, Luca Carbonaro, Ciro del Vecchio, Emanuele Pace, Giampaolo Preti, Paola Zuppella, Paolo Chioetto, Daniele Gottini, Riccardo Lilli, Antonio Scippa, Riccardo Claudi, Vincenzo Davide Cardinale, Alfonso Collura, Fabio D'Anca, Elisa Guerriero, Luisa Sciortino, Monica Rainer, Javier Pérez Álvarez, Andrés García-Pérez, Alejandro Jose Fernandez, Paul Eccleston, Andrew Caldwell, Umberto Barozzi, Iacopo Ficai Veltroni, Lorenzo Maddii, Federico Miceli, Andrea Paternoster, Federico Fiorenzoli, Dervis Vernani, Pasquale Bonfà, Daniele Brienza, Manuele Gangi, Angelo Olivieri, Elisabetta Tommasi, Antonio Jose Araiza, Andrea Bocchieri, Delphine Maryse Jollet, Ludovic Puig, Jean-Christophe Salvignol, Enzo Pascale, Giuseppe Malaguti, Giuseppina Micela, Giovanna Tinetti
Items.Title: The ARIEL telescope assembly: technical solutions and tests of an aluminum based telescope
Items.Abstract: Ariel will conduct a survey of the atmospheres of known exoplanets through transit spectroscopy. The Ariel telescope consists of an off-axis, unobscured Cassegrain telescope in the waveband between 0.5 and 7.8 µm, and operating at cryogenic temperatures. It consists of a primary parabolic mirror with an elliptical aperture of 1.1 m of major axis, followed by a hyperbolic secondary, a parabolic recollimating tertiary and a flat folding mirror. In this article, an update regarding the development of the Telescope is provided, focusing on the critical tests and technological developments, in particular: the first measurement of the WFE of a model of M1 at 0 gravity level with nm level precision, thermal conductance measurement of the mechanical interfaces of M1, details regarding the improvement in the Diamond Turning and, finally, an overview at System Level of the development of the Engineering Model of the Telescope Assembly.

Items.Authors: Brialyn Onodera, Charles R. White, Christopher Foster, Paul F. Jeffers, Kevin P. Kady, Christian Guerra, Christopher R. Sanchez
Items.Title: An update on the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope facility thermal systems
Items.Abstract: The needs of the management and control of the facility thermal systems for the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope has evolved from its inception to the system that operates today. The thermal system was designed to maintain an environment that closely matches atmospheric conditions along the optical path but, in order to meet the stringent operations schedule, several non-essential thermal systems were de-scoped prior to operations. Regular operations have granted us more clarity about the system, proving some thermal subsystems to be unnecessary and requiring the adjustment of others for energy efficiency. A thermal review was initiated and Burns & McDonnell was commissioned to review our current operations and recommend corrective courses of action to improve system efficiency and therefore efficacy. An overview of the current major facility thermal equipment operations and the recommendations for improved performance are presented herein.

Items.Authors: Eric D. Miller, James A. Gregory, Keith Warner, Beverly J. LaMarr, Gregory Y. Prigozhin, Marshall W. Bautz, Harry R. Clark, Michael J. Cooper, Kevan A. Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, WeiLin Hu, Mallory A. Jensen, Jill Juneau, Renee D. Lambert, Christopher W. Leitz, David Volfson, Douglas J. Young
Items.Title: Curving X-ray detectors for astrophysics applications
Items.Abstract: Next-generation X-ray optics will revolutionize high-energy astrophysics, yet they present several challenges to design a complementary focal plane. In particular, the focal surface is curved, requiring many small, flat sensors to achieve a large field. We present work building on MIT Lincoln Laboratory technology to curve the sensor itself, improving image quality and reducing complexity. Applying this technology to back-illuminated, large-format CCDs having well-characterized X-ray response, we describe the process and report success curving functional BI CCDs to a 2.5-m radius of curvature, achieving RMS curvature deviations less than 1 µm. We confirm that there is no appreciable increase in dark current and that the spectroscopic performance across the 0.3–6 keV band remains excellent. These results demonstrate that curved, large-format X-ray sensors are realizable, and the process can be extended to silicon detectors with other architectures, including active pixel sensors.

Items.Authors: Martin A. Barstow, Noora Alameri, Costanza Argiroffi, Miguel d'Avillez, Nigel Bannister, Joanna Barstow, Rachel Bird, Matthew Burleigh, Sarah Casewell, Elizabeth Clements, Evangelina Deliporanidou, Giulio Del Zanna, Sebastian Diebold, Jeremy Drake, Vincent Fraux, Michael Gillon, Ana Inez Gómez de Castro, Richard de Grijs, Richard Hampson, Graham Harper, Aline Hermans, Louise Harra, Jérôme Jacobs, Lionel Jacques, Christian Kintziger, Jon Lapington, Domitilla de Martino, Yaël Nazé, Hamid Al-Naimiy, Jonathan Nichols, James Owen, James Rogers, Roisin Speight, Beate Stelzer, Venkatesh Sundararaman, Mashhoor Al-Wardat, Martin Townend, Klaus Werner, Allison Youngblood
Items.Title: SIRIUS: Stellar and ISM research via in-orbit ultraviolet spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: SIRIUS is a low cost, observatory class mission developed from the J-PEX sounding rocket programme. It is a mature concept and has undergone a UKSA-funded study before being proposed for the ESA mini-F mission call. It was moved to the F3 progamme and approved for a stage 2 submission, now under evaluation. The key science goals of SIRIUS are to understand the environments in the nearby regions of the Galaxy, including study of the influence of stellar activity on exoplanet habitability, study of white dwarf atmosphere to measure composition of exoplanetary remnants and observation of the wider interstellar environment in which planetary systems exist. The instrument is a normal incidence objective grating spectrometer operating the EUV from 17 to 26 nm, with a resolving power of 5000. The main goal of the SIRIUS mission is to understand this cosmic feedback system within the Local Cavity and how it influences the habitability of our region of the Galaxy.

Items.Authors: William R. Thompson, Christian Marois, Olivier Lardière, Adam Johnson, Joeleff Fitzsimmons, Darryl Gamroth, Christopher Mann, Olivier Guyon, Julien Lozi, Tim Hardy, Simon Thibault, Frédéric Grandmont, Mamadou N'Diaye, Maaike van Kooten, Angus Bews, Krzysztof Caputa, Vincent Déo, Dylan Kerr, Andre Fogal, Kaitlyn Hessel, Garima Singh, Jean-Pierre Véran, Suresh Sivanandam, Wolfgang Heidrich, Qiang Fu
Items.Title: SPIDERS first light: self-coherent camera coronagraphy on an 8-Meter Telescope
Items.Abstract: We present first light from SPIDERS, the first dedicated instrument to demonstrate fast atmospheric self-coherent camera (SCC) coronagraphy technique on an 8-meter class telescope. SPIDERS, the Subaru Pathfinder Instrument for Detecting Exoplanets and Retrieving Spectra, works as both a classic coronagraphic imager and a focal plane wavefront sensor. Starlight is picked off by a modified focal plane mask, filtered, and reintroduced to illuminate the science focal plane with fringes. These fringes distinguish stellar speckles from astrophysical sources (i.e. planets, disk material, etc) using their mutual incoherence and enable real-time correction of any persistent speckles with a second stage adaptive optics loop. As a result, integration times for individual wavefront measurements are significantly reduced. This technology is being developed for future 8-meter class instruments including GPI2 and possible contributions to the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

Items.Authors: Ramón Navarro, Conan Butler
Items.Title: Monolithic TinyTelescope optical mechanism for PicoSat Earth  Observation: integrated release, deployment, and tip-tilt mirror design
Items.Abstract: Through this work, the space telescope Optics Mechanism required as part of the active optics for the performance of the Tiny Telescope Space Assembly (monolithic optical system within its housing, optics mechanism and camera) has been studied, design, manufacture and tested. The Tiny Telescope Space Assembly is to be used for an Earth Observation Mission, therefore its design shall be compatible with the Low Orbit space environment.

Items.Authors: Deborah M. Lokhorst
Items.Title: Building MOTHRA: how a small, remote team is delivering a facility-class telescope
Items.Abstract: We present the project management approach behind MOTHRA, a new astronomical facility now under construction. MOTHRA uses more than a thousand telephoto lenses working together to create a powerful instrument for mapping faint structures in the Universe. Although comparable to a major research telescope, MOTHRA is being built in under two years by a fully remote team of only nine people. The project spans multiple countries: management is based in North America, assembly and operations take place in Chile, and key components are sourced from suppliers around the world. Coordinating this global effort requires streamlined workflows, strong relationships with contractors, and constant, flexible communication. We outline the tools and practices that enable this rapid development, and describe our approach to managing a small, distributed team as we work toward completion in December 2026.

Items.Authors: Alicia Middleton
Items.Title: CCAT: Prime-Cam Control System and related software
Items.Abstract: Prime-Cam is one of the primary instruments being developed for use by the CCAT collaboration with the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST), which is undergoing construction at an elevation of 5600 m. Prime-Cam requires a number of hardware devices for standard operation and data collection, and so a distributed control system must be developed for controlling Prime-Cam in the field. The Prime-Cam Control System (PCS) is being developed using the Observatory Control System (OCS) framework originally developed for Simons Observatory and is adapted for Prime-Cam and CCAT-specific requirements. Within OCS/PCS, hardware devices are controlled by long-running software processes known as “agents," which are controlled by “client" scripts through the command line or frontend tools. PCS also uses various external open source software tools. This system is undergoing lab testing in preparation for deployment in 2026 for use with Prime-Cam on FYST.

Items.Authors: Dervis Vernani, Manuela Arno', Federico Fiorenzoli, Federico Folino, Paola Galli, Gabriele Grisoni, Ruben Mazzoleni, Massimiliano Rossi, Giulia Saoncella, Pasquale Bonfà, Daniele Brienza, Manuele Gangi, Barbara Negri, Angelo Olivieri, Elisabetta Tommasi, Giovanna Tinetti, Riccardo Lilli, Antonio Scippa, Emanuele Pace, Fabio D'Anca, Giuseppina Miceli, Paolo Picchi, Monica Rainer, Paolo Chioetto, Paola Zuppella, Enzo Pascale, Andrea Bocchieri, Matthias Mann, Simon Schuler, Dominik Widemann, Colin Bondet, Priscilla Viard, Umberto Barozzi, Federico Miceli, Andrea Paternoster, Andrew Caldwell, Paul Eccleston, Dale Blackmore, Gary Davies, Jack Morris
Items.Title: Making the primary mirror for the Ariel Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Ariel telescope consists of a primary parabolic mirror (M1), followed by a hyperbolic secondary (M2), a parabolic re-collimating tertiary (M3) and a flat folding mirror (M4). Media Lario is the industrial enabler in charge of the manufacturing development of the M1 mirror; made of aluminium 6061-T651, the M1 is an off-axis parabola with a big elliptical aperture having about 1.1 m major axis and 0.75 m minor axis. Among the manufacturing processes, diamond turning is the baseline process to produce the off-axis shape, followed by deterministic polishing in Media Lario and finally coated with protected silver coating by CILAS (France). The results of the development models of the M1 mirror are presented and discussed in this paper.

Items.Authors: G. Brusa, X. Zhang, S. Ragland, M. Lefebvre, J. C. Guerra, A. Cavallaro, R. Biasi
Items.Title: Adaptive secondary mirrors operation at the Large Binocular Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) adaptive secondary mirrors (ASMs) are an integral and critical part of the telescope operation. For this reason, LBT dedicates a considerable amount of effort to these mirrors. In this paper we report recent general statistics as well as more specific analysis of the operation of the two ASMs at LBT, and recent maintenance campaigns. In the operation statistics section we include down time, frequency of failing actuators, and applied flat quality, we also include an extensive analysis of the performance of the critical wind protection system. In the maintenance campaigns section, we discuss the control electronics repairs and the preventive maintenance of the liquid cooling system.

Items.Authors: Timothy R. Emeigh, Abraham D. Falcone, Kadri M. Nizam, Lukas R. Stone, Md. Arman Hossen, Laurel ONeill, Ian Ashcroft, Brynn Bortree, Sierra Deppe, Killian M. Gremling, Gavin R. Houlihan, Katie B. McWhirter, Abigail A. Raytsis
Items.Title: Development and initial characterization of next-generation event-driven hybrid CMOS X-ray detectors
Items.Abstract: The Penn State University High Energy Astrophysics Detector and Instrumentation Lab—in collaboration with Teledyne Imaging Sensors (TIS)—has developed a next-generation event-driven X-ray hybrid CMOS detector (HCD). This detector is an HCD with a 1024x1024 array of 21-micron pitch pixels, featuring a comparator in each pixel to enable event-driven readout. While the full frame operation of this detector can reach readout speeds of up to 150 frames/second, this event-driven operation allows readout of only those pixels that surpass a user-set charge threshold, enabling readout rates of up to 10 kHz. Here we report on the expected performance, initial characterization carried out by TIS, and the ongoing work at Penn State to further characterize these novel HCDs.

Items.Authors: Oscar Gonzalez, Michele Cirasuolo
Items.Title: MOONS: multi object spectroscopy for the VLT: overview, installation and commissioning update
Items.Abstract: The Multi Object Optical and Near-infrared Spectrograph (MOONS) instrument is the next generation multi-object spectrograph for the Very Large Telescope (VLT). The instrument combines the high multiplexing capability offered by 1000 optical fibres deployed by individual robotic positioners with a novel spectrograph able to provide both low- and high-resolution spectroscopy simultaneously across the wavelength range 0.64μm - 1.8μm. Powered by the collecting area of the 8-m VLT, MOONS provides the astronomical community with a world-leading facility able to serve a wide range of Galactic, Extragalactic and Cosmological studies. This paper will provide an overview of the instrument, reporting on its installation and commissioning progress in Chile as it approaches the start of operations.

Items.Authors: Youngseok Lee, Jeong-Yeol Han, Seung Ho Han, Jiwoo Lee
Items.Title: Prediction of tool influence function derived depth and volume for optical surface polishing using AI-based regression models
Items.Abstract: Nanometer-level precision polishing is essential for the fabrication of reflective mirrors used in space exploration. In this study, Artificial Intelligence (AI) was employed to support such precision polishing. Tool Influence Functions (TIFs) were generated for Cordierite, Silicon Carbide (SiC), and Aluminum–Silicon (Al-Si) materials, and regression models were constructed using the resulting material removal depth and volume data. Predictions for the two physical quantities were then performed for each material, and their accuracies were compared. The results show that the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of the volume-prediction model was lower than that of the depth-prediction model.

Items.Authors: Erika T. Hamden
Items.Title: The Eos mission, a FUV spectrograph to observe diffuse gas
Items.Abstract: With delays in NASA proposal opportunities, we report here on significant updates to the Eos mission concept, which will be proposed to the next NASA SMEX opportunity. The Eos mission will observe molecular hydrogen in nearby star forming regions and metal line emission from the CGMs of nearby star forming galaxies. Eos observes both via high resolution FUV spectroscopy, with a focus on observing faint and diffuse targets. The mission has matured while the SMEX calls have been delayed. In addition, we report on ongoing efforts by the UV group at the University of Arizona to develop UV mission concepts for a variety of funders and science cases, as well as advancement of UV detectors for use on these additional concepts.

Items.Authors: Franco Colleoni, Tomislav Vucina, Claudio Araya, John Andrew, Mario Rivera, Roberto Tighe, Juan Lopez, Doug Neill, Sandrine Thomas
Items.Title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory final coating plant integration, commissioning, and coating results over the main telescope mirrors
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory construction is done, finishing the Integration phase and starting the Commissioning phase, the Coating Plant is finally delivering its main science mirrors to the project. The M2 mirror was coated with protected Silver on 2009 and the M1M3 mirror coated on 2024 with protected Silver as well, both under the main project requirements. This paper describes the main project milestones in terms of construction, assembly, integration, and the final coating results on both mirrors. Then the main challenges in this Coating Project with a full characterization of the Coating Plant and its ancillary equipment, a characterization of the coating process with its decisions points, finishing with the future projects related to this Coating System.

Items.Authors: Benoît Horeau, Jérôme Amiaux, Clara Bataillon, Marion Baumann, Michel Berthé, Thomas Capocci, Christophe Cara, Cyrille Delisle, Elsa Ducrot, Jean Fontignie, Duc-Dat Huynh, Grégory Kaszubiak, Pierre-Olivier Lagage, Isabelle Le Mer, Nathan Leguay, Michel Lortholary, Jérôme Martignac, Thibault Pichon, Léna Provost, Bastien Reboul, Diana Renaud, Thierry Tourrette, François Visticot, Damien Bachet, Nicolas Berton, Christophe Cossou, Mickaël Lacroix, Hervé Le Provost, Virgile Meyer, Lexane Picault, Nicolas Solenne, Clémence de Jabrun, Antoine Arondel, Stéphane Correia-da-Costa, Bruno Crane, Jean-Pierre Dubois, Norma Hurtado, François Langlet, Benoît Lecomte, Antoine Maillot, Marc Ollivier, Anne Philippon, Catherine Tamiatto, Stéphane Tosti, Xueyan Zhang, Jean-Michel Reess, Yanis Gougeat, Vincent Lapeyrère, Jérôme Parisot, Eitan Pechevis, Didier Zeganadin, Alain Triffaux, Jean-Christophe Bouquier, Daphné Caillot, Fabrice Glize, Pascal Truchelut, Jean-Philippe Beaulieu, Pierre Drossart, Angèle Syty, Pierre Vigneron, Isabelle Zenone, Elisa Baldit, Pascale Danto, Gaëlle Giesen, Hervé Geoffray, Elodie Jacquel, Oceane Maisonnave, Florian Lazartigues, Jean-Christophe Salvignol, Ludovic Puig, Jorge Fiebrich, Delphine Jollet, Thierry Tirolien, Paul Eccleston, Rachel Drummond, Georgia Bishop, Davide Bruzzi, Andrew Caldwell, Martin E. Caldwell, Alexander Davidson, Lucile Desjonqueres, Salma Fahmy, Caroline Simpson, Martin S. Whalley, Keigo Enya, Enzo Pascale, Mauro Focardi, Ana Maria Di Giorgio, Sebastiano Ligori, Gianluca Morgante, Adrien Defosse, Mallaury Guerrier
Items.Title: AIRS: ARIEL IR Spectrometer development and testing towards the Flight Model
Items.Abstract: AIRS is the infrared spectroscopic instrument of ARIEL: Atmospheric Remote‐sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large‐survey mission selected as the Cosmic Vision M4 ESA mission. This mission will perform transit spectroscopy of over a 1000 of exoplanets to complete a statistical survey.   AIRS spectroscopic data will cover the 1.95-3.90 µm (Channel 0) and the 3.90-7.80 µm (Channel 1) wavelength ranges with dispersive elements producing spectrum of low resolutions R>100 in channel 0 and R>30 in channel 1. This instrument overview will mainly cover the avionic and Engineering Models. It will present updated information on the integration and testing activities which thus conduct to start the realization of the flight model.

Items.Authors: Emaad Paracha, Steven J. Benton, Aurelien A. Fraisse, Ajay S. Gill, John W. Hartley, Bradley Holder, William C. Jones, Lun Li, Richard J. Massey, Jacqueline E. McCleary, Johanna M. Nagy, C. Barth Netterfield, Susan F. Redmond, Jason D. Rhodes, L. Javier Romualdez, Jürgen Schmoll, Mohamed M. Shaaban, Sayan Saha, Bryce Warren, Jason Brown, Peter Bartosik, Ben Boyd, Pablo Trujillo, Philippe Voyer
Items.Title: From Sky to Screen - Improving File Downlinking over Error-Prone, Omni-directional Links from the Stratosphere
Items.Abstract: Long-duration stratospheric balloon missions must transmit large volumes of scientific and telemetry data over variable, omni-directional links prone to packet loss and bandwidth fluctuations. To address this, we developed a semi-autonomous file-downlink system for high-altitude astronomy missions such as SuperBIT and its successor, GigaBIT. The system comprises a payload client, ground server, and cleaner program capable of operating across UDP and TCP links. The client manages a dynamic queue of data and divides them into fixed-size chunks with metadata, enabling resumable transfers and selective retransmissions. This chunk-level approach ensures only corrupted data is resent, reducing bandwidth usage. The system helps increase overall throughput, substantially improving telemetry downlink in constrained stratospheric telescope missions. This talk presents the system design and protocol behaviour, along with the performance during SuperBIT’s final flight.

Items.Authors: Carla Crovari, Álvaro González, John Carpenter, Juande Santander, Theodoros Nakos, Juan Larrain, Aneez Mohamed, Crystal Brogan, Sean Dougherty, Elizabeth Humphreys, Shun Ishii, Takeharu Ito, Phil Jewell, George Kosugi, Norikazu Mizuno, Christian Saldias, Tzu-Chiang Shen, Kanako Sugimoto, Tom Zahorik, Martin Zwaan
Items.Title: On the road to ALMA 2030: managing and controlling a complex ensemble of interdependent but self-directed projects
Items.Abstract: The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) is now advancing the planning and preparation for the Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU), a major initiative that will enable the observatory to meet the new top-level science goals defined in the ALMA Development Roadmap.  The WSU consists of multiple interdependent projects managed at each of the ALMA Executives. These projects must progress in parallel to meet program objectives—fulfilling scientific requirements while safeguarding operations and delivering within scope, schedule, and budget.  This distributed project-management structure introduces several challenges, and traditional hierarchical control approaches are not feasible in this context. This paper presents an update on the program-level control mechanisms implemented and those currently under development. These mechanisms shift the focus from task-level verification to managing interfaces and dependencies.

Items.Authors: Christophe S. Clergeon
Items.Title: Gemini 2.0: Gemini ground layer adaptive secondary system (GLASS)
Items.Abstract: Gemini Observatory has completed an initial feasibility study for a wide-field Ground-Layer Adaptive Optics (GLAO) facility at Gemini North, which will provide a factor of two improvement in delivered image quality over a field of view greater than 6 arcminutes, for all instruments and under most natural seeing conditions whenever laser propagation is possible. The resulting concept, the Ground Layer Adaptive Secondary System (GLASS), is centered on the deployment of a new adaptive secondary mirror (ASM) and leverages major infrastructure upgrades from the ongoing Gemini North Adaptive Optics (GNAO) program. In this contribution, we present the updated system concept and performance estimates, newly expanded science case development including opportunities across Gemini North and Gemini South instruments, and refined operational scenarios (CONOPS) optimized for wide-field survey productivity.

Items.Authors: Yi Zheng, Bo Li, Bin Liang, Ying Li, Chen Xu, Ya Huang, Zhengyang Li, Xuefei Gong, Xiangqun Cui
Items.Title: Smart fabrication primary mirror of the 4.2m astrometric telescope at NIAOT
Items.Abstract: In 2024, Nanjing Institute of Astronomical Optics & Technologies was awarded the manufacturing of the Primary Mirror of 4.2-meter Astrometric Telescope. The primary is the largest aspherical mirror ever made in China. The blank is ZERODUR. It was transported to China, and mounted on the large optical fabrication machine in January 2025. A new designed 650mm active stressed lap is applied in lapping and rough polishing. And the mirror is tested using a swing arm profilometer driven by a six-joint industry robot. Both high material removal rate and shape convergence were achieved. This mirror is currently in its final phase of polishing. It is regularly measured on a dedicated interferometric test bench specifically designed to achieve the best accuracy. It is put on the vertical test tower, directly above the machine to reduce the influence of air turbulence. A novel CCOS tool was integrated with above robot to do the final finishing. The primary is now close to its final shape.
